561.title: Lucky to bear it
561.hook: not "I'm unlucky," but "I'm lucky to bear this without breaking" (Meditations 4.49)
561.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often apply the rule at the end of Meditations 4.49 to setbacks: the event is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the headland. Your line was the headland. When a wave hit, did you stand still and let it settle? Day five hundred sixty-one.

Listen to how people tell bad news. Of course it happened to me. Just my luck. Why does this always happen to me? The sentence starts before we've even decided what we think. It's almost a reflex, a little story about being the unlucky one. Yesterday Marcus Aurelius gave us the headland. In the same entry, a few lines later, he catches himself in exactly that reflex, and rewrites the sentence. Same event. Different words. And the new words change what the event is. Today: lucky to bear it.
screen: `JUST MY LUCK.` → `A REFLEX SENTENCE.` → `LUCKY TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the rewrite. Unlucky me, that this happened, Marcus imagines saying. Then he corrects himself. Not at all. Rather: lucky me, that though this happened, I'm still standing, not crushed by the present and not afraid of what's coming. Second, why that's luck. Something like this could have happened to anyone, he says. But not everyone would have come through it unbroken. So why call the event bad luck, rather than calling your steadiness good luck? Both are true. You get to choose which one is the headline. Third, the test. Then he asks the question that matters most. Does what happened stop you from being just, generous, self-controlled, sensible, careful in judgment, honest, modest, free? If it doesn't touch those, it hasn't touched what makes you who you are. Fourth, the rule to carry. Marcus ends with a sentence for every future vexation. Remember, he says: this is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune. This is not pretending. Marcus doesn't call the loss a gain. He doesn't say it didn't hurt. He moves the word luck from the event, which you didn't choose, to the bearing, which you did. That's a real shift, and anyone can try it. The flat tire is a flat tire. Changing it calmly, on the shoulder, in the rain, without taking it out on anyone: that's the part that's yours, and it's a kind of luck to be able to.
screen: `NOT UNLUCKY ME: LUCKY ME.` · `ANYONE COULD MEET IT; NOT ALL BEAR IT.` · `DOES IT STOP YOU BEING JUST?` · `BEARING IT WELL IS GOOD FORTUNE.` · then, large: `LUCKY TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one misfortune, recent or old. Say the reflex sentence to yourself first: just my luck, or why me. Notice how it feels. Now try Marcus's rewrite: this happened, and I'm still standing. Then ask his test: did it stop me from being fair, honest, kind? If not, say quietly: lucky to bear it. Notice whether anything in your body changes. The bell holds the time.
Lucky to bear it. Marcus moves luck from the event to the bearing: this isn't misfortune, but to bear it well is good fortune. Today's word.
Your line: lucky to bear it. The next time you hear yourself say just my luck, rephrase it: this happened, and I'm lucky to bear it well. Day five hundred sixty-one.

562.title: The gulf of time
562.hook: look at the vast gulf of time behind you and ahead (Meditations 4.50)
562.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes take the view of Meditations 4.50 outdoors, looking at the night sky and measuring a worry against the vastness of time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lucky to bear it. Your line was lucky to bear it. Did you catch a just-my-luck sentence and rewrite it? Day five hundred sixty-two.

Go outside on a clear night, away from the streetlights, and look up. Some of the light reaching your eyes left its star centuries ago, long before anyone alive today was born. You're looking backward in time. Plenty of people feel two things at once out there: very small, and strangely calm. Marcus Aurelius had no telescope. But near the end of his fourth book he stands at the edge of the same view, and asks what it does to the length of one life. Today: the gulf of time.
screen: `A CLEAR NIGHT, NO STREETLIGHTS.` → `LIGHT OLDER THAN ANYONE ALIVE.` → `THE GULF OF TIME.`

segments.voice: First, a plain help. Marcus calls this an unphilosophical but still useful aid against the fear of death: think of the people who clung hard to life. What did they gain over those who died young? He names a few Romans who lived long and buried many others, and then were buried themselves. The gap between a short life and a long one, he says, is small. Second, the gulf. Then the view opens. Look at the vast gulf of time behind you, he writes, and the other boundless stretch ahead. Endless before you were born. Endless after. Third, what a life measures against it. In that infinity, Marcus asks, what's the difference between someone who lives three days and someone who lives three generations? He seems to be playing on old Homer here: Nestor, the wise old king, who outlived two generations of men and ruled among the third. Against the gulf, Nestor and an infant are almost the same size. Fourth, small and calm. Some people find that view frightening. The French writer Blaise Pascal, many centuries later, wrote, in Trotter's 1910 translation: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." Marcus finds something else in it: relief. If a life is a flicker in that dark either way, then the length of it is not the thing to fight over. What matters is what you do inside your flicker. Both reactions are honest. You may feel one, or the other, or both on the same night.
screen: `THINK OF THOSE WHO CLUNG TO LIFE.` · `THE GULF BEHIND, THE GULF AHEAD.` · `THREE DAYS, OR THREE GENERATIONS?` · `SMALL, AND CALM.` · then, large: `THE GULF OF TIME.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. If it's night, go look up at the sky, or picture it if you can't. Feel the time behind you: centuries, then millennia, then more, with no floor. Feel the time ahead, just as open. Now find yourself in it: one breath, one small light. Don't try to feel anything in particular. Just notice what comes, smallness or calm or both. The bell holds the time.
The gulf of time. Marcus looks at the boundless time behind and ahead, and asks what difference three days or three generations make within it. Today's word.
Your line: the gulf of time. Look up at the night sky tonight, even for a minute, and let one worry be measured against it. Day five hundred sixty-two.

563.title: Push it away
563.hook: how easy to push away a troubling thought and be at peace at once (Meditations 5.2)
563.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 5.2 with small, everyday troubling thoughts, noticing them and setting them down; serious grief or anxiety is met in other ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gulf of time. Your line was the gulf of time. Did you look up at the sky, and what did a worry look like against it? Day five hundred sixty-three, and book five begins.

Book five of the Meditations opens with Marcus arguing with himself in bed on a cold morning, trying to get up. Anyone who has hit snooze knows that entry. The next one is shorter, and stranger. It makes a claim that sounds almost too easy: that you can push a troubling thought away and be at peace, right away. If you've ever lain awake replaying a conversation, you might laugh. Easy? But Marcus means something specific, and it's worth hearing before you laugh. Today: push it away.
screen: `MARCUS IN BED ON A COLD MORNING.` → `A CLAIM THAT SOUNDS TOO EASY.` → `PUSH IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. How easy it is, Marcus writes in the second entry of book five, to push away and wipe out every impression that is troubling or out of place, and at once to be in perfect calm. The Greek word for that calm, galene, is the word for a sea gone flat after wind. Second, what he's pushing. Not the event. Not the facts. The impression: the first picture the mind paints, before you've agreed to it. We've met this Stoic idea before. Something happens, and an impression arrives saying this is terrible. You haven't yet said yes. The push happens in that gap. Third, why he calls it easy. It's easy in the way that putting down a cup is easy. The motion is small. What's hard is noticing that you're holding it. Most of the time the troubling thought isn't something we keep on purpose. We just forget it's in our hand. Fourth, honest about the limits. Marcus isn't describing grief, or serious anxiety, or anything a person should push down rather than face. Those need time, people, and sometimes a doctor. He's talking about the everyday stuff, the stray irritation, the imagined argument, the small dread that floats in while you're doing the dishes. For those, he's saying, the first move is simply to set them down and see if you even need to pick them back up. Often you don't. And when you do need to think it through, you can choose a better time than 2am.
screen: `HOW EASY TO PUSH IT AWAY.` · `PUSH THE IMPRESSION, NOT THE FACT.` · `EASY AS PUTTING DOWN A CUP.` · `FOR THE EVERYDAY, NOT THE GRIEF.` · then, large: `PUSH IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let one small troubling thought come up: an irritation, a what-if, an old remark. Notice it as a thing you're holding, like a cup. Feel its weight for a breath. Now, on the next out-breath, set it down. Not throw it, just set it down beside you. See if the water inside you goes a little flatter. If the thought comes back, set it down again. The bell holds the time.
Push it away. Marcus says how easy it is to push away a troubling impression and be at once in calm, like a sea gone flat. Today's word.
Your line: push it away. Once today, when a small troubling thought floats in, notice you're holding it, and set it down. Day five hundred sixty-three.

564.title: Fit for you
564.hook: judge every word and act that fits you, and don't be swayed by blame (Meditations 5.3)
564.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.3 in two steps: first test an act for fairness and honesty, then, if it passes, don't let disapproval alone turn them aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday: push it away. Your line was push it away. Which small troubling thought did you notice and set down? Day five hundred sixty-four.

There's always someone ready to comment. You start eating differently and a relative has notes. You speak up at a meeting and someone rolls their eyes. You give money to a cause and a friend tells you it's naive. Sometimes the critic is right, and it's worth listening. But often the right thing simply comes with a small crowd of people who'd rather you didn't. Marcus Aurelius, who was criticized for a living, gave himself a rule for that crowd. Today: fit for you.
screen: `THERE'S ALWAYS SOMEONE WITH NOTES.` → `THE RIGHT THING HAS CRITICS.` → `FIT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the standard. Judge every word and act that is in line with nature, Marcus writes in the third entry of book five, as fit for you. For the Stoics, in line with nature meant in line with what a reasoning, social creature is made for: honest, fair, useful to others. That's the test, and it comes first. Second, the blame that follows. Don't let the blame or the talk of certain people that follows turn you aside. If a thing is good to do or say, he says, don't think it beneath you. Notice the order. You test the act first. Then, if it passes, the critics don't get a vote. Third, they have their own guide. Those people, Marcus says, have their own ruling mind and follow their own impulses. Don't keep looking over at them. That isn't contempt. It's simply that their mind is theirs to steer, and yours is yours. You can't hand your conscience to someone else's mood. Fourth, the straight road. Go straight on, he finishes, following your own nature and the common nature, because the road of both is one. What's right for you, done honestly, is also what's right for the whole. Here's the useful part. This rule doesn't mean ignore all feedback. Marcus elsewhere asks to be corrected, gladly, when he's wrong. The difference is the order. A critic with a reason gets heard, and maybe changes your mind. A critic with only disapproval doesn't get to decide what's fit for you.
screen: `JUDGE EACH ACT AS FIT FOR YOU.` · `DON'T LET THE BLAME TURN YOU ASIDE.` · `THEY HAVE THEIR OWN RULING MIND.` · `ONE STRAIGHT ROAD.` · then, large: `FIT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one right thing you've been holding back from because of a critic, real or imagined. Test it first, honestly: is it fair, true, useful? If it fails, let it go. If it passes, picture the critic's face. Let them have their own mind and their own opinion. Then picture yourself doing it anyway, calmly, without needing to win them over. The bell holds the time.
Fit for you. Marcus says test each word and act by nature; if it's right, it's fit for you, and the blame of others needn't turn you aside. Today's word.
Your line: fit for me. Do one right thing today that someone might criticize. Test it first, then don't wait for their approval. Day five hundred sixty-four.

565.title: What is wholly yours
565.hook: they can't admire your cleverness, so show what's fully yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance (Meditations 5.5)
565.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes take one quality from the list in Meditations 5.5, such as sincerity, dignity or endurance, and practice it for a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fit for you. Your line was fit for me. Which right thing did you do despite a critic, real or imagined? Day five hundred sixty-five.

Everybody has a sentence that starts, I'm just not. I'm just not a math person. I'm just not good at small talk. I'm just not creative. Sometimes it's true, and sometimes it's a door we've closed so we don't have to try. Marcus Aurelius had one too. It's a surprise to find it in the private notebook of a Roman emperor, but there it is: he thought he wasn't especially quick. And in the fifth entry of book five he turns that into a challenge. Today: what is wholly yours.
screen: `I'M JUST NOT...` → `AN EMPEROR'S OWN SENTENCE.` → `WHAT IS WHOLLY YOURS.`

segments.voice: First, the admission. People can't admire your sharpness of mind, Marcus says to himself. Fine. Whether he was being modest or honest, we can't know. But he takes it as given. Second, the turn. Then he says: there are many other things where you can't claim, I'm not built for that. So show those, the ones that are entirely in your power. And he lists them: sincerity, dignity, hard work, not chasing pleasure, being content with what you have and with little, kindness, frankness, not loving excess, not chattering, a generous spirit. Not one of them needs talent. Third, no excuse. Do you see, he asks, how many of these you could show right now, where there's no excuse of being naturally unable? And yet you stay below the mark, by choice. Then he gets even more specific. Are you forced by your nature to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your body, to try to please people, to show off, to be restless in your mind? No. You could have been free of these long ago. Fourth, slow is allowed. And if you really are slower than others, he says, then work at that too, and don't neglect it or enjoy being dull. Here's what makes this kind. Most of what makes a person good to be around doesn't depend on gifts. A slow thinker can be sincere. A shy person can be kind. A tired person can refuse to grumble. Those are wholly yours.
screen: `THEY CAN'T ADMIRE YOUR SHARPNESS.` · `SHOW WHAT'S ENTIRELY IN YOUR POWER.` · `NO EXCUSE OF NATURE.` · `IF SLOW, WORK AT THAT TOO.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MINE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Hear three of Marcus's words slowly: sincerity, dignity, endurance. Let each land for a breath. Now pick one of the three to show today. Sincerity might be saying what you actually mean in one conversation. Dignity might be not gossiping. Endurance might be finishing one hard task without complaint. Picture the moment you'll do it, and how it will look. The bell holds the time.
What is wholly yours. Marcus says that even without brilliance, many qualities are fully in your power: sincerity, dignity, hard work, kindness. Today's word.
Your line: what is mine. Show one of the three today, sincerity, dignity or endurance, somewhere no talent is needed. Day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: Nature's prescription
566.hook: as doctors prescribe cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss; take it like medicine (Meditations 5.8)
566.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes reframe a hardship as in Meditations 5.8, asking what it might be medicine for, rather than treating it only as bad luck.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what is wholly yours. Your line was what is mine. Which did you show: sincerity, dignity or endurance? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Physical therapy hurts. The stretch you're told to hold for thirty seconds feels like three minutes. The exercise for your knee is boring and sore. And yet you do it, more or less cheerfully, because someone you trust wrote it down and said: this will help. You don't argue with a prescription the way you argue with bad luck. Marcus Aurelius noticed that difference, and in the eighth entry of book five he tried to move the hard things in his life from one column to the other. Today: nature's prescription.
screen: `PHYSICAL THERAPY HURTS.` → `YOU DON'T ARGUE WITH A PRESCRIPTION.` → `NATURE'S PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: First, the doctor. People say, Marcus writes, Asclepius prescribed this man horseback riding, or cold baths, or walking barefoot. Asclepius was the Greek god of healing, and sick people slept in his temples hoping for instructions in a dream. Marcus's world was full of such prescriptions. Second, nature's prescription. In the same way, he says, the nature of the whole prescribed for this person an illness, or a disability, or a loss. The word for prescribed is the same. The event is not random, in his view. It's fitted to you, the way a prescription is written for one patient. Third, two reasons to accept it. Marcus gives two. One: it happened to you, it was assigned to you, it's woven into your own life. Two: it serves the health of the whole universe, which he believed was one living order. You don't have to share his belief about the cosmos to feel the force of the first reason. This is your life, and this is in it. Fourth, take it like medicine. So, he says, accept what happens the way you accept what the doctor orders. Many prescriptions are bitter, and we welcome them anyway, hoping for health. Here's what this changes. You can't always choose whether hard things come. But you can choose which column they go in: bad luck, to be resented, or medicine, to be taken. Taken as medicine, a hard season becomes something you can work with. Marcus isn't saying it doesn't taste bitter. He's saying bitter isn't the same as wrong.
screen: `ASCLEPIUS PRESCRIBED A COLD BATH.` · `NATURE PRESCRIBED AN ILLNESS.` · `YOURS, AND PART OF THE WHOLE.` · `BITTER, BUT TAKEN FOR HEALTH.` · then, large: `THE PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one hard thing in your life right now: an ache, a limit, a loss, a difficult person. Notice which column it's been in. Bad luck? Something to resent? Now, just for these breaths, try moving it to the other column. Picture it written on a prescription pad, with your name at the top. Ask: what might this be medicine for? Patience, humility, compassion? Take it, the way you'd take a bitter pill. The bell holds the time.
Nature's prescription. Marcus says as a doctor prescribes cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss: take it as medicine, bitter but meant for health. Today's word.
Your line: the prescription. When something hard comes today, ask: what is this medicine for? Day five hundred sixty-six.

567.title: Back to it
567.hook: don't be disgusted when you fail; return, and be glad if most of what you do is decent (Meditations 5.9)
567.tomorrow: How am I using my soul?
567.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.9 after a lapse: no self-disgust, just a return to the practice, and contentment if most of their acts are decent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nature's prescription. Your line was the prescription. When something hard came, could you ask what it was medicine for? Day five hundred sixty-seven, the end of a week.

A knitter drops a stitch three rows back. There are two ways this can go. In one, there's a sigh, a crochet hook, the stitch is picked up, and the scarf carries on. In the other, the whole thing is yanked off the needles in disgust and shoved in a drawer for a year. The dropped stitch is the same in both. The difference is the next minute. In the ninth entry of book five, Marcus Aurelius writes to himself about exactly that minute. Today: back to it.
screen: `A DROPPED STITCH.` → `PICK IT UP, OR PULL IT ALL OUT?` → `BACK TO IT.`

segments.voice: First, don't be disgusted. Don't be disgusted, discouraged or dissatisfied, Marcus tells himself, if you don't manage to do everything by right principles. Notice that he expects to fall short. A man who wrote this much about virtue knew how often he missed it. Second, return. When you've been knocked off, he says, come back again. The whole practice is in that one word. Not never fall. Return. Third, most of it is enough. And be content, he adds, if the greater part of what you do is worthy of a human being. Not all of it. The greater part. Love the thing you're returning to. Fourth, not a schoolmaster. Then a lovely detail. Don't go back to philosophy, he says, as if to a schoolmaster with a cane, but the way people with sore eyes go back to a sponge and egg, or someone goes back to a soothing bandage or a warm compress. Philosophy, for Marcus, is the medicine, not the punishment. You return to it because it helps. And look at what this week built. Lucky to bear it: luck is in the bearing. The gulf of time: a life against eternity. Push it away: set the troubling thought down. Fit for me: test the act, not the critics. What is mine: sincerity, dignity, endurance. The prescription: hard things as medicine. And now, back to it. You'll forget most of these lines by Thursday. That's fine. The practice was never to remember perfectly. It's to come back.
screen: `DON'T BE DISGUSTED.` · `WHEN KNOCKED OFF, RETURN.` · `CONTENT IF MOST OF IT IS DECENT.` · `A COMPRESS, NOT A SCHOOLMASTER.` · then, large: `BACK TO IT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one recent slip, something you meant to do or not do, and didn't manage. Notice the voice that comes with it, the disgust or the why bother. Let it speak, then let it pass. Now picture returning: the next small step back into the habit, today, as if reaching for something soothing rather than something stern. Decide what that step is. The bell holds the time.
Back to it. Marcus says don't be disgusted when you fail; return, and be content if most of what you do is worthy. Today's word.
Your line: back to it. After your next slip, skip the speech to yourself and take the next small step back. Day five hundred sixty-seven.
